title: Interior Color and Psychological Functioning in a University Residence Hall
research_question: To assess students' color preferences, satisfaction with the color and lightness level of the building they lived in, and the effects of interior color on their mood, studying activity, and orienting within a university residence hall.

participants.description: University students (230 males, 213 females) living in a university residence hall in Pisa, Italy. Mean age = 23.8 years (SD = 2.67). Mean stay at residence = 13.33 months (SD = 12.14). Participants spent an average of 6.78 hours (SD = 3.28) per day in their room (excluding sleeping time). Eight participants were excluded due to color vision deficiency.
participants.recruitment: Students living in the 'I Praticelli' university residence hall were invited to participate.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six identical university residence hall buildings, each characterized by a monochromatic interior color (violet, blue, green, yellow, orange, or red) for walls, ceilings, and floors in common spaces, and for walls/ceiling of entrance hall, one bedroom wall, and bathroom walls in student rooms. Artificial lighting was uniform across buildings (linear fluorescent bulbs, Ra ≥ 80, 3000K).

measures.instrument: Self-report choice from a color wheel (24 hues x 10 lightness levels = 240 samples)

and violet (x² = 18.13, p < 0.001)

mechanisms: Mere exposure effect (familiarity with actual color increasing pleasantness)
Residential attachment (developing connection to one's living space)
Ecological valence theory (color preferences arising from affective responses to color-associated objects, e.g., blue with clear sky/water, serenity/calm)
Perceived room height increases with ceiling lightness
Interior color increases legibility and facilitates spatial navigation
Color-emotion associations (e.g., blue with openness/peace/tranquility; red with dangers/activation)
Color-arousal modulation (long-wave colors like red/orange causing higher arousal than short-wave colors like blue/green, affecting cognitive performance via Yerkes-Dodson law)
implementation_implications: Prefer blue and green colors for university residence halls and residential settings, avoiding red, yellow, and orange.
For male students, restrict color palette to blue and green hues; for female students, allow a more varied palette including red-purple and violet hues.
Blue color is preferred in study areas.
Prefer light colors to ensure adequate lightness levels.
Prefer white ceilings over colored ones.
Using specific colors for different buildings can facilitate spatial orientation and wayfinding in complex architectural layouts.
